[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'll kick us off. i'm ethan park, ae at redwood, with maya our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: good thanks. hey. um sorry a few folks are jumping on a bit late.
[00:12] Jonah: yeah, juggling standup, but we should be fine.
[00:16] Maya: great, quick agenda. want to understand your traffic shape, latency targets, and budget constraints. then walk through levers we use to drive per‑token cost down — batching, caching, quantization, and the hosting mix.
[00:28] Priya: that's perfect. our use case: product search suggestions and checkout upsell micro‑prompts. two classes: realtime suggestions (low latency, high qps) and batching for nightly personalization. some sensitive checkout flows need PII controls.
[00:40] Alicia: SRE note — we have to keep logs for 90 days for audits and integrate with our KMS. SOC2 required.
[00:46] Ethan: got it. budget wise?
[00:48] Priya: pilot budget is tight. we can do up to $15k/mo initially, maybe more if ROI looks clear.
[00:54] Maya: ok that's useful. what's your expected token volume? ballpark.
[00:58] Jonah: under normal load maybe 20–50 million tokens a month. but peak on promo days could jump to ~100 million tokens in a burst.
[01:06] Priya: and important bit — realtime suggestions need 95th pct latency ~250–300ms end‑to‑end, including network.
[01:12] Maya: okay that helps. couple levers to hit that cost and latency: batching (larger batch sizes amortize token compute), prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts (e.g., user history), quantized model variants for cheaper throughput, and hosting routing—hosted for low-friction and dedicated to guarantee throughput.
[01:25] Jonah: can you give concrete numbers? like per‑token hosted vs dedicated?
[01:30] Ethan: sure, i'll be careful — numbers are illustrative and we'll send an exact matrix. hosted gen models are typically in the $0.0006–0.0012 per token range at small scale depending on model size and options. dedicated reserved capacity pricing amortizes to a lower per‑token compute cost in many cases — effective per‑token compute can drop to ~$0.0002–0.0005 depending on utilization and quantization. caching and batching can drive an extra 2–5x reduction in token cost for workloads with repeat prefixes.
[01:52] Priya: that's a wide band. how much of that is model license vs infra?
[01:56] Maya: split is mostly infra; model selection matters too. open models tend to be cheaper to run and can be quantized, but require validation. hosted tier includes model management and infra overhead; dedicated is more efficient per unit but you commit to a pool.
[02:09] Alicia: about caching: the KV cache stuff — our engineers are used to redis style caches. how transparent is Redwood's prefix/KV cache?
[02:18] Maya: it's automatic at the runtime layer. for repeated prefixes the KV cache reuses past key/value activations, so the backend doesn't need to recompute full attention for earlier tokens. it shows up in the console as cache hit rates and you can pin cache retention per-model. it's not the same as app-level redis; it's model internals but you can combine both.
[02:35] Jonah: and batching — what's the latency tradeoff if we wait for an 8‑request batch vs single?
[02:40] Maya: there is a tradeoff. for continuous batching we set a short collection window (e.g., 5–15ms) and target batch sizes. at low qps the batch wait can add noticeable tail latency, but once qps is above a threshold, batching reduces cost with negligible latency impact. for your 95th pct target 250ms, we often use a hybrid: dedicated pool for the realtime endpoints with batch window tuned to ~5–10ms and a hosted fallback for spikes.
[03:02] Priya: spike handling — do you have burst capacity? we can't rely on degraded UX during flash sales.
[03:07] Ethan: yes — dedicated pools can have configured burst capacity into our shared hosted layer; policy routes overflow to a slightly cheaper but higher latency fallback model. you can define SLAs per route.
[03:18] Priya: about private/VPC: we need the PII checkout flows to stay inside our VPC, keys under our KMS. how mature is the private offering?
[03:27] Maya: we have a private deployment option with a customer‑managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations. audit logs ship to your SIEM and you can choose on‑prem components if required. latency characteristics are similar to dedicated if deployed on comparable hardware. there is an additional platform fee for private deployments and a longer provisioning time.
[03:43] Alicia: provisioning time — what's realistic for a pilot?
[03:46] Maya: hosted: immediate; dedicated: 1–2 weeks to provision a reserved pool; private/VPC: 3–6 weeks depending on network reviews and certs.
[03:53] Jonah: for our budgeting exercise — if we wanted to stay within $15k/mo, with 20–50M tokens typical, what would you recommend?
[03:59] Ethan: high‑level options: 1) Pure hosted: easiest, but likely higher per‑token — might be tight at your upper volumes. 2) Dedicated small pool + hosted for overflow: better unit economics if you get ~60–70% utilization. 3) Dedicated + quantized models (int4) for the high‑QPS endpoints and hosted for experiments. Given your numbers, i'd prototype dedicated with a small reserved pool and route realtime traffic there; nightly batch jobs can run on hosted to avoid over‑committing.
[04:23] Priya: what's the math for option 2? say 40M tokens/month steady, 100M during promos.
[04:30] Maya: rough calc: assume dedicated pool amortized cost ~ $X per hour (we'll attach exact). If dedicated yields $0.0003 per token at 70% util, 40M tokens → ~$12k/month. Overflow to hosted for 60M excess tokens at $0.0008 → ~$48k so that's too high. But if you size pool for promos with burst policy, or leverage autoscale with reserved baseline + burst credits, you can cap hosted spikes to a smaller fraction. The goal is to find the committed capacity that balances reserved cost vs hosted overflow. we'll run scenario modeling in a spreadsheet.
[04:58] Jonah: so reserved capacity can actually increase cost if underutilized?
[05:02] Maya: correct. reserved pools are best when utilization is consistent. that's where our Optimize product helps — it suggests pool sizes and quantization to match workloads.
[05:11] Priya: curious about quantization quality. we won't accept regressions in suggestion accuracy. do you run evals?
[05:16] Ethan: yes, Redwood has an evals workflow where we run your prompt set against model variants and surface regressions. we can gate rollouts with automatic rollback if quality drops more than an agreed threshold.
[05:28] Alicia: security pack — does hosted store any keys? we want all keys in our KMS.
[05:33] Maya: hosted can integrate with customer KMS via federation; for full key custody you pick dedicated or private. hosted still supports encrypted-at-rest and you can opt into Bring‑Your‑Own‑Key for certain plans.
[05:44] Priya: benchmarking — we can provide a 200 prompt canonical set with typical user history. can you run a 24-hour ramp?
[05:51] Maya: yes, we'll want the prompt set and target traffic curve. we'll run 24–72 hour benchmarks across hosted/dedicated/quantized variants and return a cost/latency breakdown. we'll also capture cache hit rates so you can see savings from KV caching.
[06:05] Jonah: what's typical cache hit rate?
[06:07] Maya: depends on UI. for suggestion workflows with repeated user prefixes we've seen 30–60% hit rates; for unique prompts it's much lower. even 20% cache hits can meaningfully reduce compute.
[06:18] Priya: on observability — can we get token‑level billing mapped to routes? we need to allocate cost to product teams.
[06:24] Ethan: yes, the console exposes token breakdown per API key/route/model, with traces and latency percentiles. you can export to your billing system.
[06:33] Priya: what about retention — logs for 90 days is must. is that extra cost?
[06:38] Maya: logs beyond the default retention are an add‑on, but 90 days is a supported option on enterprise packages; we'll include that in the security pack pricing.
[06:46] Alicia: regarding SLA — what's typical?
[06:49] Ethan: for dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in enterprise contracts; hosted has published SLOs but enterprise SLA is available when you commit.
[06:58] Priya: competitor question — we've been looking at Anthropic and OpenAI. why Redwood?
[07:03] Ethan: quick: we focus on serving economics and control. you get consistent runtime primitives (KV cache, batching) and the option to run the same stack across hosted/dedicated/private. that reduces surprise costs when moving workloads. plus we do cost modeling and evals as part of pilot.
[07:17] Jonah: ok last technical — do you support custom kernel selection, or do you manage that? if we deploy private, can we tune caml kernels?
[07:26] Maya: the runtime selects kernels automatically but for private deployments we expose tuning knobs and kernel overrides for power users. you can bring your own inference stack but we recommend our runtime for observability.
[07:38] Priya: let's talk pilot scope and acceptance criteria quickly.
[07:42] Priya: acceptance criteria idea: 1) 95th pct latency <= 300ms on realtime route, 2) cost per suggestion below $0.0004 at steady state, 3) no PII leaving VPC for checkout flows, 4) access to logs for 90 days.
[07:56] Ethan: those are reasonable. we'll validate during the benchmark. for the cost target we'll run the quantized dedicated variant and show the per‑token math.
[08:05] Jonah: timeline?
[08:07] Ethan: proposed pilot 6 weeks: week 0 — config and access, week 1 — benchmark runs, week 2–4 — pilot on traffic with telemetry, week 5 — analyze and optimize.
[08:17] Priya: that fits.
[08:19] Alicia: what info do you need from us right after the call?
[08:22] Maya: prompt set, expected traffic curve for promo day, list of routes that must stay in VPC, and a contact for security review.
[08:30] Priya: we'll share those by Tuesday.
[08:33] Ethan: perfect. i'll send the pricing matrix and a sample spreadsheet showing pool sizing scenarios. maya will attach the security docs.
[08:40] Jonah: small nit — you mentioned int4 quantization. how mature is mean time between regressions?
[08:47] Maya: depends on model and prompts. we run evals per prompt set and do blind A/B to measure quality. for many generation tasks int4 is fine but for some instruction-following you might see ~1–3% drop in some metrics — that's why we gate rollouts.
[09:03] Priya: ok. one more question: do you have per-route throttles to prioritize certain routes during spikes?
[09:09] Ethan: yes, per-route policy with priority tiers. you can route low‑priority batch jobs to best‑effort capacity and keep realtime routes on reserved pools. we can also do token budget enforcement per API key.
[09:22] Priya: that is helpful.
[09:25] Maya: anything else?
[09:27] Jonah: no that's it for me.
[09:29] Priya: thanks.
[09:30] Ethan: quick recap — we will: send hosted vs dedicated vs private pricing matrix, security pack (SOC2/ISO, KMS, audit logs), run a proposed benchmark plan once you share prompt set and traffic curve, and schedule a VPC deep dive.
[09:45] Priya: yes — and we expect the pricing and docs by Monday/Tue.
[09:50] Ethan: we'll aim for Tue 2026-09-27. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep dive.
[09:58] Meeting ends.
